description: Sets electric vehicle charging fee at $5.35 per hour.

chips.text: Approved (8-2)
8 for, 2 against
Staff analysis showed demand for EV charging would drop over 50% at $5.35/hour.
Saskatoon taxpayers will subsidize the stations by $4,000-$8,000 annually.
The percentage of city vehicles that are electric was not known.
Public feedback indicated interest in using the charging stations.
Councillor MacDonald preferred $3/hour to incentivize EV adoption and align with other cities.
High fees could reduce demand, countering climate change mitigation goals.
Administration will report back in one year to reassess the charging station decision.

segments.title: Price Elasticity and Cost Recovery Analysis
description: Administration presented new analysis on price elasticity of demand.
Original analysis assumed fixed usage, leading to a $5.35 break-even.
New analysis showed demand drops significantly at higher prices.
Lowest subsidy would be at $5.45, but still wouldn't cover full costs.

chips.text: $5.35 per hour for break-even in original analysis
Councillor McDonald questioned high price compared to market
Uncertainty about actual demand at different price points

segments.title: Charging Station Enforcement and Monitoring
description: Three-hour parking limit is complaint-driven, not actively monitored.
Staff monthly visits check charger operation, not parking violations.
Complaints lead to a warning, then a ticket after three hours.
Fixing a broken charger can take up to 15 days.

chips.text: Parking services issue warnings and tickets for violations

segments.title: Program Objectives and Subsidy Trade-offs
description: Pilot project aimed to reduce transportation emissions and EV adoption barriers.
City acts as a leader and part of the solution for charging infrastructure.
Analysis shows a policy trade-off between encouraging usage and recovering costs.
Subsidies for options 4 and 5 range from $4,000 to $10,000.

chips.text: Program aims to reduce transportation emissions
$4,000 to $10,000 subsidy range for options 4 and 5
Administration plans a reassessment report after one year

segments.title: Exploring Third-Party Operator Partnerships
description: Preliminary talks with providers showed low interest for only two stations.
Scaling up the number of locations might attract third-party operators.
Administration will continue stakeholder engagement on partnerships.
No detailed discussions yet on city providing a small subsidy to operators.

chips.text: Further feasibility study on partnerships is funded
Whether a small city subsidy would attract operators

segments.title: Clarifying Enforcement and Demand Estimates
description: Residents can call the city or use a QR code to report parking violations.
Parking services mark tires and issue tickets after three hours.
The 6% demand decline estimate is based on two economist studies.
The actual anticipated demand at $5.35 per hour is uncertain.

chips.text: QR code on charging station provides reporting information
Actual demand at $5.35 per hour is unknown

segments.title: Mill Rate Impact and User Demographics
description: Original analysis assumed zero mill rate impact, but new analysis shows subsidy.
No cost-recovery rate is possible without further reducing costs.
Revenue peaks around $5-$6, with higher rates leading to higher subsidies.
Administration cannot track if users are from Saskatoon or surrounding areas.

chips.text: around $6,000 per year minimum staff costs for stations
Number of users from Saskatoon vs. surrounding areas
General Manager clarified original report assumptions on elasticity

segments.title: Private Charging Growth and Market Competitiveness
description: Private charging ports in Saskatoon increased from 30 to 70 since 2021.
City cannot meet market competitive rates with only two chargers.
Administration hasn't analyzed how many stations are needed to meet market rates.
Staff costs would likely increase with more stations, but proportionally decrease.

chips.text: 70 ports available privately in Saskatoon
Number of stations needed for city to meet market rates
Administration can do additional work on private sector delivery options

segments.title: EECS Recommendation and Option 5 Mill Rate Impact
description: Mayor clarified an EECS recommendation to seek private sector partners.
If Option 5 ($5.35/hr) is approved, mill rate impact is $4,000 to $8,000.
This is due to the updated analysis on price elasticity.

chips.text: EECS recommendation focuses on future private sector engagement
$4,000 to $8,000 mill rate impact for Option 5

segments.title: City vs. Private Charging Costs and Infrastructure
description: Saskatoon has 40 locations with 70 Level 2 chargers and 15 supercharging areas.
Private operators may have lower costs due to scale or attracting customers.
Level 2 charging is for 'top-up' convenience in public areas.
Initial infrastructure investment was $70,000, with chargers costing $12,000.

chips.text: $70,000 initial infrastructure investment
Why private operators deliver at lower costs

segments.title: Debate on Charging Options
description: Councillor Parker supported Option 4 to continue data gathering and leadership.
Councillor supported Option 5, believing users should pay for service.
Councillor Debaora supported Option 5, citing taxpayer burden and tight budgets.
Councillor McDonald supported Option 4, emphasizing city leadership and incentivizing EV adoption.

chips.text: Councillor Parker argued for Option 4 to maintain city leadership
Discussion on whether users should fully pay for the service

segments.title: Fee Approval and Third-Party Partnership Motion
description: Charging rates are not set by bylaw; council provides policy direction.
Council could direct administration to pursue partnerships with full cost recovery.
EECS recommendation for partnerships is a longer-term strategy.
Councillor Jeffries proposed a motion for administration to pursue third-party options.

chips.text: Council provides policy direction on rates, not direct approval
Administration will pursue third-party options with upset subsidy limit

segments.title: Final Comments and Votes on EV Charging
description: Councillor Pierce argued for Option 5, citing taxpayer burden and affordability for EV owners.
Councillor Davies supported Option 5 for transparency and Saskatoon residents paying for Saskatoon.
Mayor Block expressed dissatisfaction with all options due to new information.
Council approved Option 5 ($5.35/hr) and Councillor Jeffries' motion.

chips.text: Councillor Pierce argued for Option 5 to reduce taxpayer subsidy
Option 5 ($5.35/hr user fee) was carried
